H&P – Detailed

Consult Summary:
68-year-old man with known heart failure presents with 2-week worsening dyspnea and new ankle edema, consistent with acute decompensation of chronic heart failure; plan to uptitrate diuretic and arrange blood work and echocardiogram.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Progressive shortness of breath.  
• Onset/Timeline: Gradual over ≈2 weeks; markedly worse past 3 days. Now breathless walking to shops and around the house.  
• Associated symptoms: Mild dry cough; bilateral ankle swelling noticed over same few days. Feels slightly run-down.  
• Pertinent negatives: No chest pain, palpitations, fever, dizziness, or change in appetite/urination (other than usual diuretic-related frequency).  
• Exacerbating/relieving factors: Not specified.

Past Medical History:
• Chronic heart failure (date of diagnosis unspecified).  
• “Small heart attack” (likely myocardial infarction) 5 years ago; brief hospitalization, no reported ongoing angina.  
• No other chronic illnesses reported.

Medications:
• Furosemide – dose/route/frequency not documented (currently 1 tablet daily per conversation).  
• Aspirin – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Bisoprolol – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
Allergies: Denies drug allergies.

Social History:
• Lives alone with two cats (Polly, Tim).  
• Employment: Part-time lorry driver (day shifts).  
• Tobacco: Former smoker, ~1 pack/day for 25 years; quit (date not specified).  
• Alcohol: Denies use.  
• Exercise: Walks to shops daily; no other regular exercise.  
• Concern about ability to continue working if symptoms worsen.

Family History:
• Father: Died of heart attack in early 60s.  
• Mother: Alive, osteoporosis.  
• No other significant familial cardiac or pulmonary disease noted.

Physical Examination:
• Vitals: “Saturations and blood pressure are all OK” – exact values not recorded.  
• Cardiovascular/Respiratory: Examined by clinician; no specific abnormal findings documented.  
• Peripheral edema: Bilateral ankle swelling reported (no measurements).  
• Other systems: Not recorded.

Investigations:
• Ordered:  
  – Blood tests: full blood count, renal function (urea, electrolytes, creatinine).  
  – Echocardiogram to assess current cardiac function.  
• No results yet available.

Assessment & Plan:
Overall Impression:
Acute fluid overload/ decompensated chronic heart failure in setting of known CHF, precipitating increased dyspnea and peripheral edema.

DDx Integration (brief):
1. Acute on chronic heart failure – supported by history of CHF, progressive exertional dyspnea, bilateral ankle edema; no chest pain/fever.  
2. Lower respiratory tract infection – less likely; dry cough only, afebrile, chest exam “OK”.  
(No additional DDx provided by system.)

Issue 1: Decompensated heart failure  
• Assessment: Likely fluid overload; mild symptoms but impacting function.  
• Plan:  
  – Increase Furosemide from 1 tablet once daily to 1 tablet twice daily for several days.  
  – Arrange echocardiogram.  
  – Order blood tests (FBC, U&E, renal profile).  
  – Review in 1 week; sooner if worsening breathlessness, chest pain, palpitations, or dizziness.  
  – Counsel on monitoring weight, ankle swelling, and fluid intake (not explicitly stated but clinically implied – omitted to avoid inference).

Issue 2: Medication review / optimization of heart failure therapy  
• Assessment: On loop diuretic, beta-blocker, antiplatelet; doses unknown.  
• Plan: At follow-up, confirm exact doses, consider ACE-I/ARB or other guideline-directed therapy if not already prescribed (defer until medication list verified).

Issue 3: Cardiovascular risk & lifestyle  
• Assessment: Ex-smoker with strong family history.  
• Plan: Reinforce smoking cessation success; encourage gentle activity as tolerated; no alcohol issues.

General plan items:  
• Provide contact information for earlier review if deterioration.  
• Document dose change and orders in electronic medical record; coordinate echocardiogram scheduling.  

Quality checks:
● Missing: Exact vital signs, full physical-exam details, lab values, medication doses/frequencies.  
● No contradictions between transcript and absent DDx.  
● Transcript quality: Clear; occasional connectivity issues but adequate clinical information obtained.
